_readme: Golden corpus for likearr's resolver tests.
Recorded LIVE from the public MusicBrainz web service (https://musicbrainz.org/ws/2) on
September 2026, one request per 1.1s with User-Agent 'likearr-tests/0.1
(https://github.com/sysdad/likearr)'. Every release here is a real, well known public
release. Nothing in this file comes from any user's library.
What was recorded, and what was left out on purpose:
- release_groups: every release group referenced anywhere below, with its real MusicBrainz
id, title, primary credit, primary/secondary types and first release date.
- artist_release_groups: one browse page (limit 100) per artist, filtered to Album and EP
plus at most five Singles. The resolver only ever considers studio Albums and EPs from a
catalogue, so the Single cap changes no outcome; it is kept so a test can prove Singles
are excluded.
- isrc_release_groups: the release groups a recording search returns for that ISRC, filtered
to the artists in this corpus. Dropping unrelated artists changes no outcome either: the
resolver keeps only candidates credited to the same primary artist as the mapped release.
- tracklists: recorded only for the release groups the tests exercise. A release group with
no entry here answers an empty tracklist, which is what a real lookup returns for a release
group MusicBrainz has no tracklist for.
- barcodes: the real barcode of each case's representative release, used as the UPC a Spotify
album would carry.
cases maps a test name to a release group id. track_isrcs maps '<case>:<track title>' to that
recording's real ISRC.
The John Mayer Trio 'Try!' case records a release group that
MusicBrainz carries NO ISRCs for - recording/<id>?inc=isrcs answers an empty list for every
track on it - which is why no isrc_release_groups entry points at it. That absence is the
point of the case: it is what an ISRC fallback cannot reach.
Two cases record two things MusicBrainz's own typing does not
say out loud. 'Grease (The Remix EP)' (2f26958e) is typed EP with NO secondary types, so it
reads as a studio release, and it holds the ORIGINAL recording of "You're the One That I
Want" (ISRC NLF057890004) alongside the remixes - while the film soundtrack that recording
really belongs to is typed Soundtrack and credited to Various Artists. Under the 'smallest'
scope the remix EP is therefore the only candidate at all, which is the bug. 'The Feeling
(Remixes)' (d83c4c9b) is the harder half: MusicBrainz knows that ISRC from nowhere else, so
refusing the EP costs the song, and the case exists to keep that cost visible.
The Cannonball Adderley pair records the credit split behind the 'one song, two albums'
oddity. 'Mercy, Mercy, Mercy! Live at "The Club"' (28ea51ba) is typed Live and credited to
The Cannonball Adderley Quintet; 'Phenix' (579f5ca6) is a 1975 re-recording credited to plain
Cannonball Adderley, typed Album with no secondary types, and its tracklist carries the same
song title. Two MusicBrainz artists for one performer, and which one a liked copy maps to
decides which release the title fallback can even see. No rule distinguishes them, which is
what the deny list is for.
artist_relations maps an artist MBID to the artist-artist
relationships MusicBrainz records for it, in the shape artist/<mbid>?inc=artist-rels sends
(type, direction, artist). It is NOT re-recorded live: it holds the one fact
measured against the MusicBrainz API, that John Mayer (144ef525) is
a 'member of band' of John Mayer Trio (64ecce47), transcribed with both real MBIDs. The
Trio's other members are left out, as unrelated artists are elsewhere in this file.
